note: Per-class codified methodology: deterministic steps a hunter runs by hand or wires to a tool, plus an OPTIONAL ai_hook (light AI enhancement, never required) and an OPTIONAL one-line `boundary` naming the invariant two components disagree on. Keyed by {family,name} resolved to the taxonomy class id at seed time. v1.1 adds the 2026 boundary-differential pack (parser/auth/validation/cache/lifecycle/serialization/export disagreements) — the meta where two components disagree about how a request, identity, object, or response is handled. Extend incrementally.

methodologies.name: IDOR / BOLA, iterable object identifiers, sensitive data
steps: Authenticate as account A and B. Capture a request from A that references an object id (path, query, body, header, or cookie).
Swap A's object id for B's while keeping A's session/token. Read exactly one record, never the table.
Test every id surface the UI never calls: sibling endpoints, GraphQL node(id:), export/report/print variants.
Record the delta: whose data, how many records reachable, and whether write (PUT/PATCH/DELETE) also crosses the boundary.
Stop at proof. Do not enumerate; one cross-tenant read is the finding.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to cluster captured endpoints by id-parameter shape and flag which lack an ownership check in the response diff.

methodologies.name: Broken Function Level Authorization (BFLA)
steps: Recover admin/privileged routes the low role never sees: JS bundles, mobile client, OpenAPI/Swagger, docs, route manifests.
Replay each privileged action with a low-privilege session (and with no session) — change only the auth, not the body.
Try method/verb tampering and header overrides (X-HTTP-Method-Override, X-Original-URL) on blocked paths.
Confirm the action actually executed server-side (state changed), not just a 200 on a no-op.
Prove the least-damaging privileged action; do not perform destructive admin operations.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: have the model enumerate likely admin route names from the app's naming conventions in the recovered bundle.

methodologies.name: Mass assignment / over-posting
steps: GET the object and note every field the server returns (role, isAdmin, verified, balance, ownerId, emailVerified).
Add those fields to a PATCH/PUT/POST body that normally omits them.
Re-read the object to confirm the field persisted — a 200 is not proof, the stored value is.
Escalate: bind a role/owner/tenant field to take over or cross a boundary.
Report with the exact field, before/after values, and the privilege gained.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to diff the GET response schema against the accepted write body to propose over-postable fields.

methodologies.name: Cross-tenant escalation
steps: Find the client-supplied tenant selector: X-Org-Id, workspaceId, account_id, a subdomain slug, or a tenant claim in the JWT.
Create two tenants. From tenant A, set the selector to tenant B on an otherwise-authorized request.
Verify the server re-validates tenant ownership server-side, not just structurally.
Read one B record to prove the crossing; check write paths separately.
Document the selector, where it is trusted, and the blast radius across tenants.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: let the model map which endpoints echo the tenant selector unchanged vs re-derive it from the session.

methodologies.name: Full-read SSRF
steps: Find a parameter the server fetches (url=, webhook, import-by-URL, link preview, PDF/screenshot renderer).
Point it at an OOB collaborator to confirm the fetch happens and from which egress IP.
Point at 127.0.0.1 and common internal ports; diff response bodies and timings for open vs closed.
If the body returns, you have a proxy into the private network — enumerate minimally to prove reach.
Do NOT pivot further than one internal read needed to prove impact. Never touch third-party hosts.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to generate filter-bypass variants (decimal/octal/IPv6-mapped, redirect, DNS-rebind) for the specific validator observed.

methodologies.name: Cloud metadata access
steps: Confirm an SSRF primitive first (see Full-read / Blind SSRF).
Target 169.254.169.254 (AWS IMDSv1), metadata.google.internal (+ required header), and the Azure/Alibaba/Oracle equivalents; 169.254.170.2 for ECS task roles.
If IMDSv1 responds, retrieve the role name then the temporary credentials — capture only enough to prove validity.
Validate the credentials are live (e.g. sts get-caller-identity) WITHOUT touching customer data or making changes.
Report as cloud credential theft (P1) — this has stopped being a web bug. Redact the secret in the report.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: have the model identify the cloud provider from response fingerprints and name the exact metadata paths to try.

methodologies.name: Blind SSRF
steps: Trigger the fetch and confirm via OOB DNS/HTTP callback that the server reached out.
Establish an open/closed port oracle via differential timing or redirect-depth encoding.
Attempt to convert to full-read via HTTP redirect loops or error-based leakage.
Chain toward IMDS or an internal service; blind-only is a lead, not a standalone report.
Note the manual conditions still needed (e.g. IMDSv1 reachable) before claiming impact.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to design a redirect-loop payload that encodes the internal response length.

methodologies.name: SQL injection
steps: Find a parameter reaching a query; a single quote that changes the response is the first tell.
Confirm with boolean (AND 1=1 vs AND 1=2) and time-based (SLEEP/pg_sleep/WAITFOR) differentials.
For UNION, find the column count via ORDER BY, then match types.
Extract ONLY a version string or current_user as proof — never dump tables or PII.
Check second-order: store a payload in one feature, trigger it where another reads it into a query.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: have the model propose DB-specific payloads once the backend (MySQL/Postgres/MSSQL/Oracle) is fingerprinted.

methodologies.name: Server-Side Template Injection
steps: Inject a math expression into any reflected field: {{7*7}}, ${7*7}, <%= 7*7 %>, #{7*7}.
A rendered 49 identifies template evaluation; the exact polyglot that works identifies the engine.
Map engine → sandbox-escape primitive (Jinja2 config/__class__, Freemarker new, Velocity, ERB).
Prove RCE non-destructively (id / whoami equivalent) then STOP.
Test error-based/blind SSTI where a malformed expression leaks the value in an exception.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model for the minimal sandbox-escape chain for the confirmed engine and version.

methodologies.name: OS command injection
steps: Target features that shell out: file conversion, PDF/image handling, network tooling, backups.
Try separators and substitution: ; | & $(id) `id` %0a, plus argument injection (leading -).
Confirm blind execution via an OOB DNS/HTTP callback from the injected command.
Capture command output through the OOB channel or a response reflection; prove with id/hostname.
Verify non-destructively; never run commands that alter or exfiltrate data.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: let the model suggest argument-injection flags for the specific binary the feature invokes.

methodologies.name: Authentication bypass
steps: Map the auth flow end to end; look for any route to an authenticated state without valid credentials.
Test response manipulation (success:false→true), forced browsing past a step, and token-not-verified paths.
Check JWT handling: alg:none, RS256→HS256 confusion, weak secret, kid/jku injection.
Confirm you reach an authenticated action as a different user, not just a cosmetic logged-in state.
Use a throwaway/test account as the victim; never target real users.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to enumerate the state transitions in the captured flow and flag the unguarded one.

methodologies.name: OTP / 2FA brute force
steps: Request an OTP and inspect length, lifetime, and whether the attempt counter resets on resend.
Brute within the rate window; use GraphQL alias batching or parallel requests to beat per-request limits.
Check OTP-not-bound-to-user: request as yourself, submit against the victim's account.
Confirm a successful bypass reaches the protected action; stop at one proof.
Only ever brute your own test account's code.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: have the model compute the expected attempts vs the observed limit to decide if brute is in scope.

methodologies.name: Predictable password reset token
steps: Request several reset tokens in quick succession for accounts you control.
Compare them byte-by-byte: look for timestamps, counters, md5(email), or low-entropy structure.
Check Host-header poisoning: does the reset link honor an attacker Host/X-Forwarded-Host?
Check token lifecycle: reuse after login, no invalidation on new request, long expiry.
Prove takeover against your own second test account; never a real user.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to estimate token entropy and propose the generation scheme from the samples.

methodologies.name: Weak redirect_uri validation
steps: Enumerate registered redirect_uris, then test loose matching: prefix/suffix/wildcard, added path, different port/scheme.
Try bypasses: https://target.com.evil.tld, /callback/../../, a # or ? truncation, open-redirect chain.
If the code/token lands on an attacker origin, you have the takeover primitive.
Confirm the leaked code is exchangeable (or the token usable) before claiming ATO.
Chain with an open redirect on the trusted origin when direct redirect_uri is strict.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: let the model generate redirect_uri mutation candidates tailored to the observed validation rule.

methodologies.name: Race condition on a limit (limit overrun)
steps: Find a check-then-act on a limited resource: coupon, withdrawal, invite, vote, balance.
Fire ~20 identical requests simultaneously (single-packet attack over HTTP/2) to collapse jitter.
Measure STATE after, not status codes: did the balance/count exceed the server-enforced limit?
Reproduce to rule out flukes; capture the over-limit end state as proof.
Use minimal value amounts; restore/limit any real-money side effects.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to identify which of the captured endpoints share the same non-atomic counter.

methodologies.name: Payment bypass
steps: Map the full payment flow: cart → confirmation → provider callback → fulfillment.
Test client-trusted status (mark paid client-side), unverified/forgeable provider callback, test-mode key in prod.
Tamper amount/currency between quote and capture; try $0, negative, and currency-swap.
Confirm the order reaches a fulfilled/paid state without real payment.
Use the smallest possible order and reverse any side effects.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: have the model check whether the provider callback signature/timestamp is actually verified in the captured traffic.

methodologies.name: Unrestricted upload to RCE
steps: Identify where uploads are stored and whether that path is server-executed.
Bypass filters: double extension (shell.php.jpg), magic-byte prefix, content-type spoof, .htaccess/web.config, multipart filename tricks.
Retrieve the uploaded file's URL and request it to trigger execution.
Prove execution with a benign marker (echo/id) — never a full webshell on a live target.
If direct execution is blocked, chain with LFI/path traversal to include the upload.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to rank bypass techniques by the server stack fingerprinted from headers/errors.

methodologies.name: Java deserialization
steps: Spot serialized input: ac ed 00 05 magic or rO0AB base64 in a cookie, parameter, or queue message.
Fingerprint libraries on the classpath (Commons-Collections, Spring, Groovy, Hibernate) via errors/behavior.
Build a gadget chain for a confirmed library; confirm blind execution via an OOB callback.
Prove RCE non-destructively (DNS callback from the deserialized gadget) then stop.
Never run destructive gadgets on a live target.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: let the model match the fingerprinted library versions to a known-working gadget chain.

methodologies.name: Prompt injection, indirect
steps: Find content the agent ingests on someone else's behalf: a page it fetches, a doc/ticket/email, a repo file, a calendar invite.
Plant instructions in that content (including hidden/zero-width/HTML-comment text) that redirect the agent's tool calls.
Target a real capability: exfiltrate via a tool, call an internal URL (SSRF), or perform an unauthorized action.
Confirm the agent acted on the injected instruction, not just echoed it.
Prove with a benign exfil marker to a collaborator; never exfiltrate real data.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: this class IS the AI surface — use a second model to generate injection phrasings that survive the app's guardrail.

methodologies.name: Dependency confusion
steps: Harvest internal package names from lockfiles, bundles, Dockerfiles, CI logs, and error messages.
Check whether each internal name is unclaimed on the public registry (npm/PyPI/etc.).
If claimable, register a benign higher-version placeholder that only beacons on install (no payload).
Confirm the build/CI pulled your package via the OOB beacon — that beacon IS the report.
Publish nothing malicious; report immediately and request takedown.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to extract candidate internal package names from the recovered manifests and logs.

methodologies.name: Parser differentials
methodologies.boundary: Two components parse the same input differently.
steps: Find a value handled by two parsers in sequence: a validator vs an executor, a gateway vs a controller, a preview vs an import, a version-N vs version-N+1 schema reader.
Craft input that is ambiguous across them: nested vs top-level objects, duplicate JSON keys, conflicting Content-Type, trailing data, $id/$ref URI-base games, mismatched length/encoding.
Prove the disagreement: component A accepts/permits it, component B resolves a different value — observe it in a response, a side effect, or a timing/length delta.
Drive the disagreement to impact: a restriction enforced only in A is skipped in B (local-file read, auth skip, SQL built from the B-value).
Stop at one proven differential with the exact divergent bytes. Do not fuzz the whole grammar; name the two components and the value each saw.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to diff the two parsers' accepted grammar from their code/specs and propose the smallest input each reads differently.

methodologies.name: HTTP parameter pollution (HPP)
methodologies.boundary: Authorization and business logic read the same parameter from different sources.
steps: Identify a parameter that appears in more than one place: query + body, duplicate names, path + query, JSON + form.
Submit conflicting values (id=victim in one source, id=self in another; role in query vs body).
Determine which source the permission check canonicalizes and which the downstream query/operation consumes — they are often not the same.
If authz reads the allowed value but execution reads the attacker value, you have crossed a boundary: prove one unauthorized read/write or one injected query.
Report the exact duplicate parameter, which component read which copy, and the single resulting impact. Stop at proof.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: have the model list, per framework, the precedence rule for duplicate params (first/last/array) so you predict the split before testing.

methodologies.name: Broken Object Property Level Authorization
methodologies.boundary: The object is yours to touch; a specific property is not.
steps: GET an object you own and inventory every property (role, owner, tenant, balance, status, verified, internal flags).
Separate read-exposure (a property returned that should be filtered) from write-exposure (a property accepted that should be server-controlled).
On write, include the sensitive property with a changed value; on read, request representations/fields the UI never asks for (GraphQL field, ?fields=, export).
Re-read to confirm the property's stored value actually changed, or that the extra property actually came back — a 200 is not proof.
Prove one property crossing (privilege or cross-tenant) and stop; do not sweep every field destructively.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to diff the GET schema against the write-accepted body and the admin schema to flag server-controlled properties that leak or are writable.

methodologies.name: Header-based authorization bypass
methodologies.boundary: A trusted header means one thing at the edge and another at the origin.
steps: Enumerate headers the stack trusts for identity/routing: X-Forwarded-For, X-Original-URL, X-Rewrite-URL, X-Forwarded-Host, X-HTTP-Method-Override, X-User-Id, X-Internal, custom gateway headers found in JS/config.
Request a protected path and inject each header alone, changing nothing else.
Watch for the edge enforcing a rule the origin re-derives from the header: path shown as X-Original-URL, IP allowlist satisfied by X-Forwarded-For, method swapped by override.
Confirm the privileged action executed server-side (state changed / data returned), not a cached or no-op 200.
Report the single header, the component that trusted it, and the one action it unlocked. Stop at proof.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: let the model infer from response/timing which header the origin honored vs the edge stripped.

methodologies.name: Inconsistent state across services
methodologies.boundary: What one service validated is not what another service stored or executed.
steps: Map a flow that spans services/steps: validate here, persist there, or sync A→B asynchronously.
Submit a value that passes validation but differs from what gets committed (validated slot vs persisted time, eligibility vs applied discount, quoted price vs charged amount).
Read the persisted/downstream state directly and compare it to what validation approved.
Prove the gap has value: a booking/charge/quota that validation would have rejected now exists.
Record validated-value vs persisted-value side by side. One proven divergence is the finding; do not loop it.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to trace, from code or traffic, where validation output and the persistence write diverge in the request lifecycle.

methodologies.name: Workflow step skipping
methodologies.boundary: A later step assumes an earlier one validated, but each step trusts the client's claim of progress.
steps: Record the full multi-step flow (cart→address→payment→confirm; invite→verify→activate) and the token/flag each step sets.
Replay a late step directly, forging or reusing the state the earlier step would have set (status=paid, verified=true, step=3).
Check the server re-derives progress server-side rather than trusting the submitted marker.
Prove a terminal state reached without its precondition: provisioned without payment, activated without verification.
Stop at the one skipped gate that yields value; document the exact step bypassed.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: have the model enumerate the intended state machine and flag which transitions are only enforced client-side.

methodologies.name: Web cache deception
methodologies.boundary: The cache and the origin disagree on whether a response is personal or public.
steps: Find an authenticated, personalized endpoint (profile, dashboard, API returning your data).
Append a path/extension the CDN caches by rule but the origin ignores (/account/x.css, ;.js, /..%2f, cache-busting suffix) and request it while authenticated.
Check the response for Cache-Control: public (or cacheable) with your personal data and no Vary: Cookie.
From a clean, unauthenticated client, request the same crafted URL and confirm the victim's cached response is served.
Prove exactly one leaked personal field to a second identity. Do not harvest; the single cross-identity read is the finding.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to diff cache directives between the normal and the suffixed URL and rank which suffixes the observed CDN caches.

methodologies.name: Suspended, deleted or unverified account still authorized
methodologies.boundary: A security decision made once is not re-enforced as state changes over time.
steps: Establish an authorized context (valid session, token, collaborator invite, active role).
Revoke it through the legitimate path: log out, change password, remove the collaborator, downgrade the role, delete the resource, expire the invite.
Replay the previously authorized request/token after revocation — including background jobs, cached permissions, and long-lived API tokens.
Confirm access still works post-revocation: read or act where the new state should forbid it.
Prove one access that should be denied; note the revocation event and the surface that ignored it. Stop there.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to list every place the app caches an authorization decision (JWT claims, session store, edge, job queue) that a revocation must invalidate.

methodologies.name: Time-of-check to time-of-use
methodologies.boundary: The state checked is not the state used, because something changed in between.
steps: Find an operation that checks a condition then acts on it non-atomically (balance check then debit, ownership check then move, quota check then create).
Identify the window: a second request, a slow validation, an async job, a retry/cancel path that mutates state between check and use.
Drive the state to change inside the window (parallel request, flip ownership, exhaust/refill the resource) so the check passes against stale state.
Confirm the action used the stale decision: a debit that overdrew, a move that bypassed ownership, a create past quota.
Prove one TOCTOU with the interleaving written out. Keep it minimal — single overrun, not a stress loop. (See also race-on-a-limit.)
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to point at the check→use gap in the handler and name the concurrent mutation that invalidates the check.

methodologies.name: Cross-tenant PII leakage
methodologies.boundary: Data hidden in one representation leaks through another surface.
steps: List every surface that can expose the same records: REST, GraphQL, search/autocomplete, RSS/export/archive, profile pages, mobile API, admin preview.
Take a field restricted or filtered in the primary UI and request it through each alternate representation.
Look specifically for a surface that forgets the tenant/ownership filter the main path applies (search index returns other tenants, export ignores scope, autocomplete reveals hidden names).
Confirm the leaked data belongs to a different tenant/user, not your own echoed back.
Prove one cross-tenant record via the weakest surface; name the surface and the filter it dropped. Do not enumerate the dataset.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to enumerate, from the API surface, every representation of a given resource so you test the one the devs forgot.

methodologies.name: Mutation XSS (mXSS) and sanitizer bypass
methodologies.boundary: Markup that is safe when sanitized becomes active when the browser re-parses it.
steps: Locate a rich-text/HTML field that is sanitized server- or client-side then re-inserted (innerHTML, template rehydration, editor reconstruction).
Submit payloads that survive the sanitizer as inert but mutate on re-parse: namespace confusion (SVG/MathML/foreignObject), broken comments, attribute/entity reinterpretation, template normalization.
Trigger the re-parse path the sanitizer does not model (editor reopen, preview render, copy-paste normalization) and watch for execution.
Confirm script actually runs in the victim's origin, and whose session executes it (self vs another user vs admin).
Prove one firing payload in the context that has impact; capture the pre- and post-mutation markup. Stop at execution.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to generate mXSS vectors tuned to the specific sanitizer and DOM-insertion sink you observed.

methodologies.name: Stored XSS, privileged user with privilege elevation
methodologies.boundary: Content stored by a low-trust actor is rendered, and trusted, in a high-privilege session.
steps: Find content a low-privilege or outside actor can store that an admin/privileged user later views (attachment attrs, names, notes, collaborator fields).
Trace the full path: input → storage → serialization → the privileged UI's rendering sink. Watch for a representation change during editing that re-exposes a legacy HTML-insertion path.
Land script that executes in the privileged session (mind CSP/nonce propagation across frames — a propagated nonce can re-enable execution).
From the privileged context, perform one authenticated action that elevates: grant your account a role, change a permission — the chain to takeover is the impact.
Prove the elevation once with a benign marker action; do not exercise destructive admin operations. Write the full low→admin chain.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to map which stored fields reach an admin-only view and which rendering sink there is unsanitized.

methodologies.name: HTTP/2 downgrade smuggling
methodologies.boundary: The front end and back end disagree on where one request ends and the next begins.
steps: Confirm an H2 front end that downgrades to HTTP/1.1 at the back end (the rewrite is where length/framing disagreements are introduced).
Probe H2-specific desync: pseudo-header and header-name injection (CRLF in an H2 header value), content-length vs implied length mismatches, TE handling after downgrade.
Send a crafted request and prove a second, smuggled request was prefixed onto the next connection's victim request (observe the poisoned response or a controlled reflection).
Escalate within scope: cache poisoning, request hijack, or an internal path reached through the smuggled prefix.
Prove one reliable desync with the exact framing; never pivot into other tenants' live traffic beyond the minimum proof.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to enumerate H2→H1 rewrite quirks for the identified front-end proxy and suggest the smallest desync primitive.

methodologies.name: CSV / formula injection
methodologies.boundary: Data that is inert in the app is executable in the export's destination.
steps: Find a field you control that flows into an export (CSV/XLSX report, invoice, conversion log, emailed template).
Store a formula-leading value (=, +, -, @, or tab/CR prefixes) that the app treats as plain text.
Export and open in the target consumer (spreadsheet app) to confirm the cell is interpreted as a formula, not a string.
Show real impact for the destination: DDE/command launch on open, or exfiltration via a formula that fetches a URL (WEBSERVICE/HYPERLINK) to a collaborator.
Prove one interpreted cell with a benign marker; name the field, the export, and the consumer. Do not ship a working command payload.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model which export formats the target emits and the exact formula prefix each target spreadsheet engine auto-evaluates.
